title.narrative: Fueling Green Recovery in Armenia – advancing forest infrastructure and creating sustainable jobs for rural communities

description.narrative:
The Project’s activities will be implemented in the following 8 marzes: Tavush, Shirak, Gegharkunik, Kotayk, Aragatsotn, Armavir, Ararat, Vayots Dzor (capital city of Yerevan and 2 remaining marzes of Syunik and Lori covered by GCF funded SAP014 “Forest resilience of Armenia, enhancing adaptation and rural green growth via mitigation” project and implemented by FAO are not included). Comparative overview of Activities/interventions foreseen by SAP014 “Forest resilience of Armenia, enhancing adaptation and rural green growth via mitigation” and Proposed Project are visualized in the table below:
[https://formioblob.blob.core.windows.net/formio/uploads/table1-58e4a5bc-5d64-4f92-a330-811b4231274c.png?st=2021-11-24T09%3A57%3A13Z&se=2022-11-24T11%3A37%3A13Z&sp=r&sv=2018-03-28&sr=b&sig=toZ%2Fv6maMf32G2ba50UOjk8iUvng4CBHNZQnXpKFx5Y%3D]
According to information provided by the Ministry of Environment planting of 150 ha per year is financed from the state budget. Currently, there are no other projects supported by donors that target afforestation and reforestation activities (Other than SAP014 “Forest resilience of Armenia, enhancing adaptation and rural green growth via mitigation”).
Selection of beneficiary regions has been carried out taking into account: 1) poverty level of rural population and availability of unemployed due to the Covid-19 outbreak population (return migrants, employees of MSMEs that suspended their operations, households suffered due to drastic decrease of remittances’ flow), 2) results of preliminary mapping carried out by the Ministry of Environment in 2020 aimed at identification of potential plots for afforestation and reforestation activities (e.g. within the framework of “Planting 10 mln trees” Project delayed due to pandemic). The map of identified sites, to be finalized during the inception stage of the Project along with identification and training of beneficiaries, is attached (Annex I.). This map includes 120 plots from 3 to 40 ha (total 1300 ha), located in 50 municipalities.
The following selection criteria will be used:
[https://formioblob.blob.core.windows.net/formio/uploads/table2-4e735260-54ab-4b6e-9193-07557c0063d3.png?st=2021-11-24T09%3A58%3A59Z&se=2022-11-24T11%3A38%3A59Z&sp=r&sv=2018-03-28&sr=b&sig=MblYFUm%2FwfcRHyGn6cAKxohQYJbCRSWzsSrNFwcd9RM%3D]
The overall goal of the project is to contribute towards leveling up (by 2030) the national capacities and infrastructures necessary for meeting the country's goal of increasing Armenia’s forest cover to at least 20% by 2050.
The overall objective of the project is to scale up afforestation/reforestation capacities of the key national actors through the advancement of forest infrastructure (20 mln seedlings to be supplied annually by 2030) and expanding employment and self-employment opportunities for vulnerable populations (minimum 3,500 sustainable jobs) leaving in the adjacent areas.
Component 1. – Advancement of afforestation, reforestation, restoration activities, and sustainable forest management
Sub-component 1.1. Advancement of national forest infrastructure – will be aimed at the establishment of 1) “Seed bank” under the aegis of Hayantar SNCO, 2) 8 greenhouses (1,000 square meters each – one in each beneficiary marz) within the structure of Hayantar SNCO capable to supply 4,000,000 container seedlings annually, 3) 2 greenhouses (1,000 square meter each – in 2 beneficiary marzes) within the structure of Armenia Tree Project Charitable Foundation capable to supply 1 mln container seedlings annually, 4) 1 greenhouse (300 square meters) within the structure of My Forest Armenia Foundation capable to supply up to 200,000 container seedlings annually, 5) establishment of 1,000 backyard nurseries (150 square meters in average that could supply around 6,000 seedlings annually and generate additional revenues for the targeted households) in the vulnerable municipalities of targeted regions. Outcome 1.1. – Increased capacities (by the end of the Project’s Y2) secure supply of 20,000,000 seedlings (6mln of which container seedlings and 8,8 existing capacities) annually.
Complementarity with national programs and ongoing/planned Projects supported by partner international organizations and donor agencies will advance the overall framework for sustainable forest management with a specific focus on the regional and municipal actors. More specifically, Armenia Tree Programme Charitable Foundation is currently implementing Project funded by the EU that aimed at embedding municipal greening practices throughout small regional towns and communities, as well as designing/launching models for private sector engagement.
Sub-component 1.2. Establishment of 1,300 ha of the forests in the mountainous areas – In addition to the current rate of afforestation and reforestation activities implemented by 3 partner organizations (around 300 ha per year), each partner will carry out establishment (from 2nd to 5th year of the project) of around 400 ha of the forests. In total, this will account for around 4 mln trees. Outcome 1.2. – 4 mln trees are planted and 1,300 ha of forests are established at the land plots in the mountainous areas (by the 5th year of the Project implementation).
Component 2. Establishment of sustainable employment/self-employment opportunities for the vulnerable population leaving in deprived municipalities adjacent to the forest areas – Increased capacities of the 3 key partner organizations will lead towards additional afforestation/reforestation activities (in total, during the 5 years of the Project 1,300 ha of forests in mountainous regions will be established), which in its turn will secure around 500 sustainable and green workplaces in the targeted regions. The establishment of the 1,000 backyard nurseries (based on the review of statistical data from the Armenian Tree Project that so far helped to establish 200 such nurseries) will secure employment for 1,000 people and result in additional revenues for households equivalent to 2,000 USD annually (which is a significant augmentation to the income sources for the rural households). Also, other types of “non-timber” employment opportunities via MSMEs in the rural areas (such as collection of berries and fruits, tourism and recreation activities, and others to be identified during the Full Proposal design stage) will be secured for 2,000 people and supported through support to the establishment of collection centers, encouraging private sectors matchmaking and collaboration, a public-private partnership with the engagement of business support organizations, sectoral and regional business associations and agricultural cooperatives. Outcome 2. – 3,500 sustainable and green jobs are established by the end of the Project’s Y3.
One of the main tendencies in the sector that has been recorded during recent years is the increasing role and ratio of non-government actors (e.g. Armenia Tree Project and My Forest Armenia Foundation) in afforestation/reforestation activities. Currently accounting on average around 50% of the total volume of tree planting, this indicator has been doubled during recent 3-4 years. The main reason behind such phenomenon is the increased interest of private sector companies towards financing such activities (to reduce the carbon footprint of their operations) and the advanced infrastructural capacities of the non-government players.
The proposed Project will level up the combined capacities to supply seedlings (by reaching 20 mln seedlings per year) and fully eliminate the need for importing them during planned large-scale plantings. Promotion of the concept of “carbon neutral operations” (being currently discussed with relevant stakeholders), bringing in responsible private sector companies will greatly contribute towards the transformation of the afforestation/reforestation drivers, ensure paradigm shift and increase the share of private-sector funded engagements.
Also, the demonstration effect of the successfully piloted “backyard nursery” concept (around 200 households participated in the initial round launched by the Armenian Tree Project) has contributed towards the increased interest of other rural households which are eager to be engaged. Serving as a vivid example of a “green recovery” instrument (green jobs and increased climate resilience), this practice will lead towards 1) increased share in supplies of seedlings (6 mln per year, which makes around one-third of the total supply), 2) competitive instrument for reducing rural income poverty by providing additional and sustainable income for the households.
EPIU will fulfill the role of both Accredited and Executing Entities. Accredited to GCF in 2019 (and to Adaptation Fund in 2016), EPIU has substantial experience and expertise in the management of projects of a similar scale and with a particular focus on afforestation/reforestation. Currently executing two big projects funded by AF (with the total budget close to the 5 mln USD) in the climate adaptation domain, EPIU will be serving as Executing Entity for the GCF funded SAP014 “Forest resilience of Armenia, enhancing adaptation and rural green growth via mitigation” Project implemented by FAO.
The following 3 organizations with which EPIU has a well-established partnership framework will be serving as implementing partners: 1) “Hayantar” State Non-Commercial Organization operating under the aegis of NDA and responsible for the management of Armenian forest resources, 2) “Armenia Tree Project” Foundation – diaspora supported charity that during recent 25 years implemented significant activities in afforestation/reforestation domain, and 3) “My Forest Armenia” Foundation – another diaspora driven initiative that has been established recently and poised to become one of the leading non-public sector operators.
Potential risks have been categorized into the following:
Risks with Project Management and Designing:
Likelihood: Low
Impact: Medium
Ø Risks with project’s inception mapping would take more time than expected to design and implement;
Ø Risks in identifying and defining an appropriate logical framework and tentative output;
Ø Priorities may change on existing project program by NDA;
Ø Internal transfer/posting of project management personnel;
Ø Internal and external influence on decision making and resource allocation;
Ø Potential conflict of interest in procurement;
Risk mitigation measures
Ø Ensure real-time coordination and comprehensive understanding regarding objectives and timeline activities of the Project among implementing partners and other concerned stakeholders;
Ø All types of decisions regarding Readiness Proposal will be approved by the Project Steering Committee (PSC);
Ø Highly competent officials will be nominated for Procurement Evaluation Committee (PEC);
Ø PSC will regularly be provided with real-time updates about project management personnel;
Risks with Budget Implementation
Likelihood: Medium
Impact: Medium
Ø Mismatch in component-wise budget allocation.
Ø Potential change in the procurement cost and other resources.
Ø Inappropriate disbursement schedule.
Risk mitigation measures
Ø Procurement of consultants and other resources will be accomplished within the stipulated timeline;
Ø Comprehensive disbursement schedule will be formulated compatible with component-wise implementation.
The Project will also integrate the existing staff of the EPIU with a dedicated M&E Unit that will be in charge of monitoring and evaluation, of the E&S safeguards, and reporting/advising for the EPIU. The M&E unit will also have the mandate to ensure respect of the Gender and Environment Action Plan including the promotion and execution of intense training for EPIU and partners’ staff members focusing on gender mainstreaming and the prevention of sexual harassment or any harassment for that matter as well as abuse of authority.
The project will be monitored via (i) Georeferencing ensuring a unique link between the project’s activities and geographical coordinates and allowing stakeholders to ensure clear identification of activities and beneficiaries. (ii) Field data Collection: Field data will be collected by the Forest Monitoring Center and by the M&E unit via dedicated activities planned with communities. To this end, the M&E unit will collect data with and from communities following the approach and specifications identified for the development of baseline. (iii) Geospatial analysis: the M&E unit - supported by the Forest Monitoring Center of the MoE and by the EPIU - will monitor activities and processes thanks to remote sensing and photointerpretation analysis via drones available at the MoE. The combination of georeferencing, ground-truthing, monitoring with communities, and remote sensing analysis will allow stakeholders, including the GCF, to have a clear understanding of the project’s effectiveness and efficiency. Additionally, the described approach will allow the M&E unit to advise and support the EPIU management enhancing the project’s capacity to deliver and support stakeholders in the decision-making processes.
EPIU as an accredited entity will ensure annual reporting to the GCF. The report will include also the audit report that will be commissioned by EPIU to an independent firm. The project’s reporting will consist of four elements: (I) Technical Reports (TRs) prepared by Implementing Partners. TRs will describe executed activities and involved beneficiaries according to M&E indicators. Implementing Partners and service providers will ensure Georeferencing of each executed activity and will present TRs quarterly to the M&E expert; (II) Quarterly reports (QRs) prepared by the M&E unit for EPIU Director. QR will present the work and achievements of activities. It will include - among other - data and information from the beneficiaries and other involved stakeholders. QR is prepared by the M&E unit for the EPIU and will contribute to the annual report; (III) Annual reports (ARs) prepared by the M&E unit for the PSC and EPIU. ARs will present the work and achievements reported by the M&E unit via the QRs and will include implementation and fiduciary chapters. ARs will include findings and recommendations of EPIU supervision reports (SRs). ARs will include as well independent annual audit reports (AARs) and the “Project’s Implementation Atlas” presenting the maps and charts obtained thanks to the georeferencing of project activities. Both will be presented as annexes of the AR. ARs are prepared by the M&E unit, validated by EPIU director, and validated by the PSC, and are transmitted to the GCF.
